```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(kableExtra)

crime <- read_csv("group number 2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

crime <- crime |>
  mutate(
    reported_date = as.Date(`date reported`),
    reported_year = year(reported_date),
    reported_month = floor_date(reported_date, "month"),
    campus = case_when(
      university == "Michigan State University" ~ "Michigan State",
      university == "Ohio State University" ~ "Ohio State",
      university == "Texas Christian University" ~ "TCU",
      university == "University of the Pacific" ~ "Pacific",
      university == "University of Central Florida" ~ "UCF",
      university == "Stetson University" ~ "Stetson"
    )
  )

# A shared 2018–2024 period is used for the descriptive figures.
sample <- crime |>
  filter(reported_year >= 2018, reported_year <= 2024)

monthly <- sample |>
  count(campus, reported_month)
```

# Abstract (Executive Summary) - Xueying Luo

This report examines changes in reported campus crime following online sports betting legalization using 55,218 crime log entries from six universities across California, Florida, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas. We analyze monthly crime reports from January 2018 through December 2024 and compare average monthly reports during 24-month periods before and after selected state policy dates. We find that reported incidents decreased by 22.7% at Michigan State University, from 118.2 to 91.4 per month, while Ohio State University experienced a smaller decline of 1.0%, from 246.4 to 243.8. In contrast, the University of Central Florida (UCF) experienced a 3.2% increase, from 67.5 to 69.7 reports per month, and Stetson University experienced a 39.5% increase, from 7.9 to 11.0. California and Texas, where online sports betting remained illegal, also experienced changes in campus crime reporting. Overall, the results show no consistent pattern in reported campus crime following the selected policy dates. These descriptive comparisons do not establish whether legalization caused the observed changes.

# Data - Xueying Luo & Pei Yun Chuang

Our primary data source consists of 55,218 campus crime log entries from six universities in five U.S. states. The data were provided for the Simulation Week assignment and include Michigan State University (17,175 records), Ohio State University (21,022), Texas Christian University (TCU) (3,817), the University of the Pacific (3,378), the University of Central Florida (8,848), and Stetson University (978). The original logs cover different time periods and use different reporting formats. To make comparisons more consistent, we focus our main analysis on January 2018 through December 2024, which includes 40,196 records across the six universities.

The harmonized dataset contains nine variables: reported date, occurrence date, reported time, occurrence time, state, university, crime category, sports betting legalization date, and crime location. Each observation represents an entry in a university crime log rather than a unique victim or necessarily a confirmed criminal offense. Because universities may differ in how they record and report incidents, differences in the number of entries should not automatically be interpreted as differences in underlying crime rates.

## Cleaning and main measures - Xueying Luo

We cleaned each university's crime log separately before combining the six datasets. First, we standardized the reported and occurrence dates to `YYYY-MM-DD`, times to `HH:MM`, and state names to two-letter abbreviations. We then grouped the original incident descriptions into six categories: Alcohol offense, Sexual offense, Robbery offense, Burglary offense, Assault offense, and Other. The Other category includes incidents such as theft, property damage, and other reports that do not fall within the five specified offense categories. We also reviewed duplicate entries and inconsistent dates and crime classifications. We removed exact duplicate source records where appropriate but retained separate incidents that shared the same information after harmonization. When an occurrence date appeared incorrect and could not be verified from the original log, we retained the incident and treated the occurrence date as missing.

Our main outcome is the number of campus crime reports recorded each month. We calculate this measure using the reported date rather than the occurrence date because all 55,218 entries contain a reported date. The monthly counts therefore describe changes in reported incidents, which may not reflect the exact timing of the crimes themselves. The final dataset contains 816 missing occurrence dates, 1,330 missing reported times, 2,539 missing occurrence times, and 62 missing locations. We preserve these missing values rather than replacing them with estimated information. The legalization date is also missing for 7,195 records from California and Texas because neither state had legalized online sports betting during the period examined.

We use a consistent observation period from January 2018 through December 2024 to examine monthly reporting patterns across the six universities. For the before-and-after analysis, we compare average monthly crime reports during the 24 months before and after selected state policy dates. Michigan's online sports betting launch date is January 22, 2021, and Ohio's is January 1, 2023. For Florida, we use May 25, 2021, which represents a legal authorization milestone rather than the beginning of uninterrupted online sports betting availability. We exclude the policy month for Michigan and Florida to avoid comparing partial months. Because Florida's betting availability changed after its initial authorization, its before-and-after results require additional caution. These comparisons describe changes in campus crime reporting around the selected dates rather than the causal effects of legalization.

## Cleaning review for Michigan State, Ohio State, and TCU - Pei Yun Chuang

I reviewed the harmonized records for Michigan State University, Ohio State University, and Texas Christian University (TCU), the three institutions assigned to me for the initial data-cleaning stage. The three sources differ in their original date, time, and offense-description formats, so the combined file uses the shared nine-column schema. In the combined dataset, these universities contribute 17,175, 21,022, and 3,817 entries, respectively. I checked that their university names and state abbreviations are consistent (MI, OH, and TX), and that the reported dates can be parsed for the monthly analysis.

A limitation of the harmonized file is that distinct original incidents can have identical values after only the nine retained fields are kept. Consequently, matching rows in the combined CSV are not sufficient evidence to delete an incident. Missing source details should remain missing rather than be inferred. This review describes the combined output; the original source-to-cleaned transformations should be checked separately before claiming that every individual cleaning decision has been independently reproduced.

## Summary statistics - Pei Yun Chuang

Table 1 describes differences in monthly reporting across the six universities. Each university has 84 observed months from January 2018 through December 2024, and the statistics use reported incidents rather than enrollment-adjusted crime rates. Ohio State recorded an average of **226.7 reports per month**, with a standard deviation of **86.4** and a monthly range of **29 to 563**. Michigan State averaged **121.7** per month (standard deviation **66.7**), while Stetson averaged **9.7** (standard deviation **6.5**). These differences partly reflect the different sizes and reporting systems of the institutions. Because we do not divide counts by student enrollment, Table 1 should not be read as a ranking of campus safety.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-monthly
#| tbl-cap: "Monthly campus crime reports, January 2018–December 2024"
monthly_stats <- monthly |>
  group_by(campus) |>
  summarize(
    Mean = round(mean(n), 1),
    `Standard deviation` = round(sd(n), 1),
    Minimum = min(n),
    Maximum = max(n),
    Months = n()
  )

kbl(
  monthly_stats,
  col.names = c("University", "Mean", "Std. dev.", "Minimum", "Maximum", "Months")
) |>
  kable_styling(position = "center")
```

*Table 1 note:* The unit of observation is a university-month. All 84 months from 2018 through 2024 contain reported incidents at each university. Statistics are calculated from monthly counts, not individual crime records. Higher counts do not necessarily indicate higher crime rates per student.

# Findings/Results - Xueying Luo & Pei Yun Chuang

## Monthly incident trends differ across universities - Xueying Luo

Monthly campus crime reports followed different patterns across the six universities, making it difficult to identify a common change around sports betting policy dates. Figure 1 shows monthly reports from January 2018 through December 2024, with red dashed lines marking the selected policy milestones. Ohio State and Michigan State generally reported more incidents than the other four universities. However, several campuses experienced declines before their policy dates. For example, Michigan State's annual reports fell from 1,940 in 2019 to 896 in 2020, while Ohio State's declined from 2,786 to 2,241. UCF also recorded fewer reports in 2020 (687) than in 2019 (978). These declines coincided with COVID-19 disruptions to campus activity, although the crime logs alone cannot explain their causes. Overall, the differences across universities and over time suggest that changes in campus reporting cannot be attributed to sports betting policies alone.

```{r}
#| label: fig-monthly
#| fig-cap: "Monthly Reported Campus Incidents and Sports Betting Policy Milestones, 2018–2024"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

policy_dates <- data.frame(
  campus = c("Michigan State", "Ohio State", "UCF", "Stetson"),
  policy_month = as.Date(c(
    "2021-01-22",
    "2023-01-01",
    "2021-05-25",
    "2021-05-25"
  )),
  label = c(
    "Jan 22, 2021",
    "Jan 1, 2023",
    "May 25, 2021",
    "May 25, 2021"
  )
)

monthly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reported_month, y = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(
    data = policy_dates,
    aes(xintercept = policy_month),
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = policy_dates,
    aes(
      x = policy_month,
      y = 480,
      label = label
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "red",
    size = 3,
    angle = 0,
    hjust = -0.1,
    vjust = 0
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~campus) +
  labs(
    x = "Month Reported",
    y = "Number of Reported Incidents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Note:* The figure shows monthly campus crime reports at six universities from January 2018 through December 2024. The horizontal axis represents the reporting month, and the vertical axis represents the number of reported incidents. All panels use the same vertical scale. Red dashed lines indicate the selected online sports betting policy dates, with the corresponding dates labeled beside each line. Michigan and Ohio mark the launch of online sports betting, while Florida marks legal authorization rather than uninterrupted online betting availability. Pacific and TCU have no policy lines because online sports betting remained illegal in California and Texas during the study period. The figure is descriptive and does not establish a causal relationship between sports betting policies and reported campus incidents.

## Before-and-after comparisons do not show a common direction - Xueying Luo

Average monthly campus crime reports changed in different directions following the selected sports betting policy milestones. Figure 2 compares reported incidents during the 24 months before and after each state's selected policy date. Michigan State's monthly average declined from 118.2 to 91.4 reports, a 22.7% decrease. Ohio State experienced a much smaller decline, from 246.4 to 243.8 reports per month, or 1.0%. In contrast, both Florida universities recorded increases. UCF's monthly average rose from 67.5 to 69.7 reports (3.2%), while Stetson's increased from 7.9 to 11.0 (39.5%). Stetson's percentage increase was relatively large because its average before the policy date was only 7.9 reports per month. The Florida comparisons also require caution because the selected 2021 date marks legal authorization rather than the beginning of continuous online betting availability. Overall, these differences do not show a consistent increase or decrease in campus crime reporting following the selected policy milestones.

```{r}
#| label: fig-before-after
#| fig-cap: "Average monthly reported incidents before and after selected sports betting policy milestones"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

before_after <- monthly |>
  mutate(
    period = case_when(
      campus == "Michigan State" &
        reported_month >= as.Date("2019-01-01") &
        reported_month <= as.Date("2020-12-01") ~ "Before",
      
      campus == "Michigan State" &
        reported_month >= as.Date("2021-02-01") &
        reported_month <= as.Date("2023-01-01") ~ "After",
      
      campus == "Ohio State" &
        reported_month >= as.Date("2021-01-01") &
        reported_month <= as.Date("2022-12-01") ~ "Before",
      
      campus == "Ohio State" &
        reported_month >= as.Date("2023-01-01") &
        reported_month <= as.Date("2024-12-01") ~ "After",
      
      campus %in% c("UCF", "Stetson") &
        reported_month >= as.Date("2019-05-01") &
        reported_month <= as.Date("2021-04-01") ~ "Before",
      
      campus %in% c("UCF", "Stetson") &
        reported_month >= as.Date("2021-06-01") &
        reported_month <= as.Date("2023-05-01") ~ "After",
      
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  mutate(period = factor(period, levels = c("Before", "After"))) |>
  group_by(campus, period) |>
  summarize(
    average = mean(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

before_after |>
  ggplot(aes(x = campus, y = average, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    x = "University",
    y = "Average monthly reported incidents",
    fill = "Period"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

*Note:* Each bar represents the average monthly number of reported incidents over a 24-month period. Michigan State compares January 2019–December 2020 with February 2021–January 2023. Ohio State compares January 2021–December 2022 with January 2023–December 2024. The University of Central Florida and Stetson compare May 2019–April 2021 with June 2021–May 2023. Florida's selected policy date represents legal authorization rather than uninterrupted online betting availability. The figure presents descriptive comparisons and does not identify causal effects.

## The Other category accounts for most incidents - Pei Yun Chuang

The third finding is that the broad **Other** category makes up most of the harmonized reports. Figure 3 separates incidents into the six categories used across all campuses. Of the **40,196 reports in the 2018–2024 analysis period**, **31,703** are classified as Other. This category includes several source offense types rather than one consistent kind of crime. Therefore, comparisons of overall incident counts may depend on differences in what each university records, and analyses of a specific crime category may be more informative than total reports alone.

```{r}
#| label: fig-crime-type
#| fig-cap: "Reported incidents by crime category and university, 2018–2024"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
sample |>
  mutate(`crime type` = factor(`crime type`, levels = c(
    "Alcohol offense", "Sexual offense", "Robbery offense",
    "Burglary offense", "Assault offense", "Other"
  ))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `crime type`)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ campus, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Crime category", y = "Number of reported incidents") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

*Figure 3 note:* Each panel shows the numbers of reported incidents by category for one university from 2018 through 2024. The Other group includes many different original incident descriptions. The vertical scale differs across panels and counts are not adjusted for campus enrollment.

## Crime reports also change in states without legalization - Pei Yun Chuang

The final finding is that crime reports also change at universities in states without online sports betting legalization. Figure 4 displays annual reports at Pacific and TCU, located in California and Texas. Both universities show year-to-year variation despite the absence of a state online sports betting launch during the observation period. These campuses offer useful context, but they do not function as matched statistical controls because their populations, reporting systems, and underlying crime trends may differ from the legalized states. The variation in these comparison campuses further limits a causal interpretation of Figure 2.

```{r}
#| label: fig-no-legalization
#| fig-cap: "Annual reported incidents at Pacific and TCU, 2018–2024"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
sample |>
  filter(campus == "Pacific" | campus == "TCU") |>
  count(campus, reported_year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reported_year, y = n, color = campus)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year reported", y = "Number of reported incidents", color = "University") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*Figure 4 note:* Annual counts reflect the dates incidents were reported, not necessarily when they occurred. The lines include only Pacific (California) and TCU (Texas). These are counts of log entries, not rates per enrolled student.

# Conclusion - Pei Yun Chuang

Reported campus crime changed in different directions around the selected state sports betting milestones. Michigan State and Ohio State recorded lower monthly averages afterward, whereas UCF and Stetson recorded higher averages. Similar variation at Pacific and TCU, which did not have online sports betting legalization dates in the study period, suggests that many other factors can influence campus reports. Our data cannot isolate the effect of legalization because the crime logs use different reporting practices, we do not observe changes in enrollment or campus activity, and the observation period includes pandemic disruptions. Florida also presents a timing problem: its 2021 authorization did not provide continuous online betting access. A useful next step would be to compare specific offense categories and crime reports per enrolled student, using consistently defined online betting launch dates and additional information on campus conditions. Our results establish differences in reported counts, not a causal effect of sports betting legalization.
